title: What certification do drinking water treatment and distribution operators need in the US?
description: US drinking water operator certification: SDWA section 1419, EPA's 1999 guidelines and nine baseline standards, with Texas TCEQ rules as a worked example.
shortAnswer: Operators of community and nontransient noncommunity public water systems in the United States must be certified under a state program that meets the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) operator certification guidelines published on February 5, 1999 under section 1419 of the Safe Drinking Water Act. The guidelines require classified systems, validated exams, renewal every three years or less with approved training, and a certified operator in responsible charge. Noncompliant states lose 20 percent of their revolving fund grant.
keyTakeaways: There is no federal operator license. Section 1419 of the Safe Drinking Water Act (42 U.S.C. 300g-8) directed EPA to publish minimum standards, and states run the programs.
EPA's Final Guidelines (64 FR 5916, February 5, 1999) set nine baseline standards, with state compliance from February 5, 2001.

States must classify systems by potential health risk, require exams with validated questions, a high school diploma or GED (or approved substitution) and increasing experience by class, and a designated certified operator available for each operating shift.
Renewal must be on a fixed cycle of no more than three years with state-approved training, and anyone whose certificate has been expired for more than two years must be reexamined.

In Texas, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) issues three-year licenses and requires ten hours of approved continuing education per year of license validity, two of them resiliency training for licenses expiring on or after April 1, 2024.
jurisdiction: United States (federal framework, with Texas as the worked state example)
regulator: US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Office of Water, with state drinking water programs; in Texas, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ)
appliesTo: Owners of community water systems and nontransient noncommunity water systems
Operators in responsible charge of treatment facilities and distribution systems
Operating personnel who make process control or system integrity decisions about water quality or quantity that affect public health
State drinking water programs that administer operator certification

sections.heading: Who sets drinking water operator certification rules in the US?

blocks.text: States set and enforce the rules, within a federal framework. [Section 1419 of the Safe Drinking Water Act](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/300g-8), added by the 1996 amendments, required EPA to publish guidelines specifying minimum standards for certification and recertification of operators of community and nontransient noncommunity public water systems, taking into account existing state programs, system complexity and system size.

The enforcement lever is money. Beginning two years after the guidelines were published, EPA must withhold 20 percent of the funds a state would otherwise receive under the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund unless the state has adopted and is implementing a program that meets the guidelines. EPA's [Final Guidelines](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/fr/64/5916) state that withholding is the only sanction for state programs that do not meet them.

The guidelines cover two types of system defined in them. A community water system serves at least 15 service connections used by year-round residents or regularly serves at least 25 year-round residents. A nontransient noncommunity system regularly serves at least 25 of the same people over six months per year, such as schools, day care centers, factories and hospitals.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects section 1419 as codified at 42 U.S.C. 300g-8 and EPA's Final Guidelines (64 FR 5916, February 5, 1999) as at November 2026. EPA published additions in 2001 on program review and withholding, and the Expense Reimbursement Grants program for small system operator training ended on December 31, 2012. The Texas rules cited are current on the Texas Administrative Code as amended effective March 23, 2025.

sections.heading: What are EPA's nine baseline standards for state programs?

blocks.text: Every state program must include the essential elements of nine baseline standards. The guidelines mark essential elements with words such as "the States must" and recommended elements with "the States should". The nine standards are:

items: **Authorization:** legal authority, evidenced by an Attorney General's certification, to require certification of operators of all community and nontransient noncommunity systems.

**Classification of systems, facilities and operators:** classify systems by indicators of potential health risk, require an operator in responsible charge certified at or above the system's classification, certify all personnel making process control or system integrity decisions, and require a designated certified operator to be available for each operating shift.
**Operator qualifications:** pass an exam with validated questions, hold a high school diploma or GED (or approved substitution), and have the defined on-the-job experience for each class.
**Enforcement:** regulations requiring system compliance and the ability to suspend and revoke certifications for misconduct such as fraud or gross negligence.
**Certification renewal:** state-approved training requirements based on certification level and a fixed renewal cycle of no more than three years.
**Resources:** sufficient resources to fund and sustain the program.
**Recertification:** a process, including review of experience and training and reexamination, for anyone whose certificate has been expired for more than two years.
**Stakeholder involvement:** ongoing involvement in program revision and operation, beyond public comment on rules.
**Program review:** periodic reviews of regulations, exam items, enforcement, training relevance and data management.

blocks.text: The guidelines also contain an antibacksliding rule: EPA will not approve a state program that reduces its standards below the level that existed 12 months before the guidelines took effect, unless the state justifies the reduction and EPA approves it.

sections.heading: What must an operator do to become certified?

blocks.text: Under baseline standard 3, an operator must pass an exam, meet an education requirement and have class-appropriate experience. All exam questions must be validated, which the guidelines define as independently reviewed by subject matter experts to ensure the exam is based on a job analysis and related to the classification of the system or facility.

The education requirement is a high school diploma or GED, and states may allow experience or relevant training to substitute. The experience requirement increases with each classification level, and post high school education may substitute for experience, with credit possible for related fields such as wastewater. The same education, training or experience cannot be counted toward both the education and the experience requirement.

The validated exam definition links directly to a [job task analysis](/guides/how-to-conduct-a-job-task-analysis) and an [assessment blueprint](/glossary/assessment-blueprint), which is the same discipline a utility can apply to its own internal competency checks.

sections.heading: How often must operators renew certification?

blocks.text: States must run a fixed renewal cycle of no more than three years, and all operators, including grandparented operators, must complete the amounts and types of state-approved training the state sets for their certification level. An individual who fails to renew or qualify for renewal within two years after the certificate expired must recertify.

Recertification under baseline standard 7 requires a review of the individual's experience and training and reexamination. The guidelines state plainly that an individual is not certified with an expired certificate.

Grandparenting, where a state chose to allow it, was limited to existing operators in responsible charge of existing systems that had to have a certified operator for the first time. The system owner had to apply within two years of the state regulation taking effect, the certificate is site specific and non-transferable, and it lapses if the system is reclassified to a higher level.

sections.heading: How does a state apply the guidelines? The Texas example

blocks.text: Texas runs its program through the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) under 30 Texas Administrative Code Chapter 30, Subchapter K. Under [30 TAC 30.381](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/texas/30-Tex-Admin-Code-SS-30-381), a person who performs process control duties in the production or distribution of drinking water for a public water system must be licensed, unless exempt, and must comply with the state's public drinking water rules in Chapter 290.

[30 TAC 30.390](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/texas/30-Tex-Admin-Code-SS-30-390) sets qualifications for Class D, C, B and A licenses, each requiring an examination, with separate surface water, groundwater and distribution tracks at Class C and B. Applicants for Class C or B must earn at least half of their experience in the specific field. College hours or training credits can substitute for experience: 16 semester hours or 20 additional training credit hours equal six months, up to one year for Class C and two years for Class B and A.

Licenses are valid for three years under 30 TAC 30.30 unless a subchapter specifies otherwise. To renew, [30 TAC 30.392](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/texas/30-Tex-Admin-Code-SS-30-392) requires approved continuing education equal to ten hours per year the license is valid, two of which must be resiliency training for licenses expiring on or after April 1, 2024, and the Resiliency Overview Course must be taken once. Under 30 TAC 30.24, renewal training must be completed within the current license term and excess hours do not carry over.

Texas also limits Class D renewal. A Class D license is not renewable for operators at groundwater treatment systems of 250 connections or more or serving 750 people or more, at surface water treatment systems, or for supervisors of distribution systems with more than 250 connections, which pushes those operators to a higher class.

blocks.text: Duties here fall on three parties: the water system owner, the individual operator, and the state program. sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models a utility's system classifications, operator classes and process control tasks as a framework, then maps continuing education to the concepts each class must maintain. That lets a training manager show which renewal hours address which operating risks, rather than counting hours alone.

faqs.q: Is there a national drinking water operator license?
faqs.a: No. Section 1419 of the Safe Drinking Water Act directed EPA to publish guidelines, and each state runs its own certification program. Requirements such as classes, exam content and renewal hours vary by state, within the minimum standards in EPA's 1999 guidelines.

faqs.q: Does a small water system need a certified operator?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is a community or nontransient noncommunity system. The guidelines require states to classify all such systems and require an operator in responsible charge certified at or above the system's classification. A certified operator must be available for each shift, which the guidelines define by system size, complexity and source water.

faqs.q: What does available mean for the shift operator requirement?
faqs.a: The guidelines define available as, based on system size, complexity and source water quality, a certified operator being on site or able to be contacted as needed to initiate appropriate action in a timely manner. It does not always require physical presence.

faqs.q: Can Texas continuing education hours carry over to the next license term?
faqs.a: No. Under 30 TAC 30.24, approved training used to renew a license must be completed after the issuance date and before the expiration date of the current license, and training credits completed beyond the amount required for that renewal period do not carry over.
